faq.a: If CT is unavailable, treat as ischemic stroke with aspirin after excluding hypoglycaemia and obvious bleed, and arrange urgent transfer.
faq.q: Can stroke be treated without CT?

faq.a: Because cerebral perfusion may depend on higher pressures; only lower if >220/120 mmHg.
faq.q: Why avoid aggressive BP lowering in acute ischemic stroke?

faq.a: When SAH is suspected and CT is negative or unavailable; look for xanthochromia.

exam: A 58‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden right‑sided weakness; CT unavailable – what is your immediate management? — Check glucose, give aspirin after ruling out bleed, control BP, arrange transfer.
How does a hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage differ from an ischemic stroke in early management? — Prioritise BP reduction, avoid antiplatelets, consider surgical referral.
What bedside sign helps differentiate subarachnoid haemorrhage from migraine? — Neck stiffness and photophobia with sudden thunderclap headache.
Why is aspirin contraindicated in a patient on warfarin with INR 3.5 presenting with stroke? — High INR indicates bleeding risk; give vitamin K and reverse anticoagulation first.
In a patient with sickle‑cell disease and acute focal deficit, what extra cause should you consider? — Cerebral vaso‑occlusion; manage with hydration, analgesia, and possible exchange transfusion.
What are the key components of secondary prevention after a first ischemic stroke in a low‑resource setting? — BP control, aspirin, statin, lifestyle advice, HIV/TB screening.

A patient with HIV on ART develops sudden left‑sided weakness; CT shows a small deep bleed – what is the likely cause and next step? — HIV‑associated vasculopathy; control BP, avoid anticoagulants, arrange neurosurgical review.
How would you explain a normal early CT in a patient with classic stroke symptoms? — Early ischemic changes may be invisible; repeat imaging or MRI later, treat clinically.
ai.title: Neurovascular Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Neurovascular disorders encompass stroke, intracranial aneurysm and arteriovenous malformation. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical patterns and limited imaging, with urgent management aimed at preventing brain injury.

b: Sudden focal deficit or altered consciousness
Headache of sudden onset, especially with vomiting
sections.p: Acute loss of neurologic function due to impaired blood flow (ischemic) or bleeding (hemorrhagic) in the brain. Diagnosis is clinical first, supported by CT or MRI when available.

t.b: Is it hemorrhagic or ischemic? Hemorrhage appears hyperdense; normal early CT suggests ischemia.
Is there large vessel occlusion or aneurysm? Guides reperfusion or surgical referral.

t.a: Bedside NIH Stroke Scale (or adapted local scale)
t.b: How severe is the deficit? Guides urgency of reperfusion therapy.
Are there papilledema or retinal hemorrhages indicating raised intracranial pressure?

b: NIHSS 0‑4: minor
NIHSS 5‑15: moderate
NIHSS >15: severe
sections.p: Ischemic stroke severity is staged by NIHSS; hemorrhagic stroke by Glasgow Coma Scale and volume of bleed.

t.b: Level of consciousness; ≤8 signals need airway protection.

b: Ischemic: large‑artery atherosclerosis, cardio‑embolism (rheumatic mitral disease, atrial fibrillation), small‑vessel disease, HIV‑associated vasculopathy.
Hemorrhagic: hypertensive intracerebral bleed, ruptured berry aneurysm, malaria‑related cerebral malaria, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion.
sections.p: Identify the most common aetiologies, especially those prevalent in East Africa.

b: Sudden unilateral weakness, speech difficulty → middle cerebral artery.
Sudden severe headache, neck stiffness → subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Progressive weakness, seizures → intracerebral hemorrhage.
sections.p: Pattern of deficits points to vascular territory; timing and associated symptoms help differentiate ischemic from hemorrhagic.

b: Blood glucose to rule out hypoglycaemia.
Full blood count, coagulation profile if bleed suspected.
sections.p: Prioritise bedside tools; use imaging when possible; know alternatives when unavailable.

t.b: Is hypoglycaemia causing the deficit? <2.8 mmol/L confirms need for glucose.
Are there coagulopathies that increase bleed risk? Prolonged PT/INR suggests warfarin effect.

t.a: Lumbar puncture (only if CT unavailable and SAH suspected)
t.b: Is xanthochromia present? Confirms subarachnoid bleed.

b: Decreasing level of consciousness
Severe hypertension >220/120 mmHg
Seizure at onset
sections.p: Identify life‑threatening features that demand immediate action.

b: Airway protection if GCS ≤8.
Blood pressure control: IV labetalol or nicardipine for hypertensive bleed; avoid aggressive lowering in ischemic stroke unless >220/120 mmHg.
Antiplatelet (aspirin) for non‑cardioembolic ischemic stroke after 24 h if no bleed.
Anticoagulation for cardio‑embolic stroke (e.g., warfarin) once hemorrhage excluded.
Surgical referral for large intracerebral bleed or ruptured aneurysm.
sections.p: Treat the underlying vascular event, control secondary injury and prevent recurrence.

b: Blood pressure control – target <140/90 mmHg.
Statin therapy for atherosclerotic disease.
Antiretroviral therapy adherence in HIV‑positive patients.
Screen for sickle‑cell disease and provide hydroxyurea where feasible.
sections.p: Long‑term risk reduction focuses on modifiable factors common in low‑resource settings.

b: Hypoglycaemia – check glucose first.
Seizure with post‑ictal paralysis (Todd’s paresis).
Brain tumour presenting with acute deficit.
Early CT may be normal in ischemic stroke – repeat if deficit persists.
Elevated blood pressure may be reactive; do not assume primary hypertension.
Normal coagulation does not rule out anticoagulant effect from newer agents (e.g., DOACs).
